summary.title: gifbot - Building a GitHub App
summary.one_liner: You learn how a webhook-driven GitHub bot differs from a GitHub App and how to convert one, using installation access tokens from a signed JWT.
takeaways: GitHub Apps have their own identity, avoid personal access tokens and bot accounts, and can be installed across many repos with one click.
Each App webhook event includes an installation ID, and rate limits apply per installation.
To act as an App, sign a JWT with the App ID and private key (RS256), then request an installation access token from the /installations/{id}/access_tokens endpoint.
The bot's comment logic stays largely the same; only the token used for API calls changes.
summary.summary: The post, written shortly after GitHub Apps left beta in 2017, walks through building gifbot, a Node.js bot that replies to comments containing [gifbot:search] with a Giphy GIF. It first shows the original webhook-plus-personal-access-token version and lists its limitations, such as acting under the owner's identity and per-repo manual setup. It then covers converting the bot into a GitHub App, using jsonwebtoken to sign a JWT and exchanging it for an installation token. The code samples are short and the author explains each step.
